questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Finite Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis
questions.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(\frac{1}{2}y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032052/assets/29cf73562152cb8201c8e93545ca7f8416aa8412217cfc9dcdaf87e5b794d971.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=2.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(2)^{3}}{3}-0)-(\frac{(2)^{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis by First Rewriting the Function
questions.problem: Find the area between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{x+1}{4}},$ the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=-1$ and $y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{x+1}{4}} \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{x+1}{4} \\ 4{y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & =4{y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4{y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{0}-y{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =(0-1)-(0+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-2|=2.$

questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=16-{y}^{4}$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}16-{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{4} & =16 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032052/assets/488788313bd32999611a520ec26e4ba6fd68a56e0333a7252a0faaf7107cad90.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=16-{y}^{4}$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=-2$ to $y=2.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(16-{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =16{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-2}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =16\cdot y{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =16\cdot (2-(-2))-(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-2)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =64-\frac{64}{5} \\  & =\frac{256}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Finite Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y({y}^{4}-16) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y({y}^{2}-4)({y}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y(y-2)(y+2)({y}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032052/assets/03737836a352eafaf486e7e5f71d882ac39715e788a0c9113eb809b185584bdc.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-2$ to $y=0.$
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}(\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{16}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y-3{\int }_{-2}^{0}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{-2}^{0}-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(0-(-64))-\frac{3}{2}(0-4) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis by First Rewriting the Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+\frac{1}{4}} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+\frac{1}{4} \\ x & ={y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}({y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}\,|}_{-2}^{-1}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot y\,{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-4)-\frac{1}{4}[-1-(-2)] \\  & =-\frac{15}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So, the area that we want is

$$
A=|-4|=4.
$$
